flashcards.definition: Lift a heavy printer with two people, remove all packing strips and supports before switching it on, and if it came from the cold, leave it off a few hours to prevent condensation.
Near a power outlet and network port with no cables to trip on, on a stable flat surface out of direct sunlight, well ventilated, easy to reach, and access-controlled for confidential printing.
The interface between the print device and the operating system, usually installed by Plug and Play; every client OS needs a suitable one, and a 64-bit OS needs a 64-bit driver.

reference.title: Printer Drivers and Page Description Languages

flashcards.definition: HP's page description language, tied more closely to specific printer models so output can vary by device, but usually faster than PostScript; often chosen for large volumes of office text.

reference.title: Printer Drivers and Page Description Languages

flashcards.definition: Adobe's device-independent page description language, giving consistent output across devices but usually slower than PCL; commonly used for graphic design and desktop publishing.

reference.title: Printer Drivers and Page Description Languages

flashcards.definition: Controls printing, scanning, and network connectivity on printers and multifunction devices; update it from the control panel or web interface to fix bugs and security flaws, after backing up settings and testing on one device.

flashcards.definition: A printer's wired link through its RJ45 port; it gets an IP address from DHCP or is set by hand, often at its control panel, and a DNS entry lets clients reach it by name.
A printer's link over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth instead of a USB or Ethernet cable.
A printer with no access controls, so any guest can use it; even guest printing today often adds network segmentation, user authentication, or a guest Wi-Fi network.

A printer installed on one computer and shared from the Sharing tab of its Printer Properties, under a share name; users with permission connect from Network in File Explorer by right-clicking it and choosing Connect.
Printing on both sides of the paper, chosen on the Finishing tab of Printing Preferences; the printer component that does it automatically is installed or configured in Printer Properties.
Whether pages print in portrait or landscape; set the default on the Finishing tab of Printing Preferences, or change it for one job with the Properties button in the application's Print dialog.
The default paper type set for each of the printer's paper trays, configured in the Printer Properties dialog along with hardware options such as a duplex unit or finisher.
Chosen on the Paper/Quality tab of Printing Preferences, where economy or draft mode saves ink or toner; the same tab sets the paper size and type.
Lets only authorized accounts submit print jobs: set permissions on the Sharing and Security tabs of Printer Properties, or have the printer check users itself, locally or against a directory server.
A way to release a secured print job: the user presents an ID badge to the printer's smart card reader, instead of typing a PIN on the control panel.

Records of each print job, kept by the print server or printer, showing which users and devices printed what; they help track missing documents, and syslog can send a printer's logs to a central server.
The printer holds a job until the user authenticates at the device, by PIN or badge, reducing the risk of confidential pages being taken from the output tray.
Features of a networked multifunction device or scanner that direct scan output to a destination: an email attachment, a shared network folder (SMB), or a cloud storage service.
A network scan service that sends the scan as an email attachment; the device needs the IP address of an SMTP server, which typically authenticates the user before sending.
A network scan service that saves the scan to a shared network folder; the device needs the path to the file server and share, and users need write permission to the share.
A network scan service that uploads the scan to a cloud storage service such as OneDrive or Dropbox; users sign in to their cloud accounts through the scan dialogs.
A scanner type that passes the paper over a fixed scan head, which makes it efficient for scanning documents with many pages.
A scanner type that shines a bright light on an object placed on a glass surface and uses mirrors and a lens to create a bitmap file of it.
A printer that uses a laser, a light-sensitive drum, toner, and a fuser; popular in offices for its low cost, quiet operation, speed, and high-quality output, in grayscale or color.
The laser printer's toner supply; the printer warns when toner is low, and to replace it, remove the new cartridge's packing strips, rock it gently to spread the toner, and install it right away.
A set of replacement laser printer parts, typically feed rollers, a transfer roller, and a fuser unit, installed when the printer's internal page count triggers a Maintenance Kit Replace message.
Works out the right print density or color balance, basically how much toner to use; most printers do it automatically, but if output looks wrong, run it from the control panel or driver.
Unplug it and let it cool, then wipe away dust and toner with a soft cloth or toner-safe vacuum, never compressed air or a household vacuum, and clean rollers with 99% isopropyl alcohol.
The light-sensitive drum, usually inside the toner cartridge, where the laser forms the page as an electrostatic image that attracts toner; echo images mean it is not being cleaned properly.
A printer that sprays tiny ink droplets onto paper, often used for color photos; cheap to buy but costly to run, and slower and noisier than a laser printer.

Holds an inkjet's ink, with sensors that detect the ink level; a color printer needs at least four reservoirs, for cyan, magenta, yellow, and black, and the driver prompts you to replace an empty one.
The inkjet part that sprays the ink, by heating it into a bubble that bursts (thermal) or with a piezoelectric element; most thermal heads are built into the ink cartridge.
An inkjet's paper rollers: a load roller moves the top sheet in, a separation roller keeps extra sheets out, and eject rollers send the page to the duplexing assembly or output bin.
The inkjet's paper feed, usually one input tray that is smaller than a laser printer's and needs restocking more often; a stepper motor advances each sheet as the print head makes its passes.
Fixes missing lines in inkjet output caused by a blocked or dirty nozzle: run the printer's cleaning cycle from its property sheet or control panel, then try inkjet cleaning products if needed.
Calibrates an inkjet's print head when output is skewed, using the function on the printer's property sheet; it usually runs automatically when you replace the ink cartridges.

A printer that uses a heating element to create images; the common direct thermal type, which usually needs special thermal paper, prints barcodes, labels, and receipts, at speeds measured in inches per second.
In a thermal printer, a stepper motor turns a rubber-coated roller that friction-feeds the paper, in fanfold or roll form, through the print mechanism.
Paper containing chemicals that react and change color when heated by the printer's heating element, creating the image; most direct thermal printers require it.
Use the right size and type for the model, insert the roll with its shiny, heat-sensitive side facing out, and check that the print head holds the paper end when you close the case.
The part that heats the special paper so it changes color and forms the image; clean the print head with an isopropyl alcohol swab or a cleaning card to remove sticky residue.
Tearing receipts across the serrated teeth makes paper dust and debris, so remove the buildup with a vacuum or soft brush, and clean off any stuck labels.
A printer that strikes an inked ribbon against the paper, such as a dot matrix printer with a column of pins in its print head; still used for invoices, pay slips, and multipart forms.
Layers of paper with carbon or carbonless coating between them, so an impact printer makes duplicate or triplicate copies in one pass; usually continuous, tractor-fed paper.
The inked ribbon the print head strikes to mark the paper, usually in a cartridge that slots over the print head carriage; when print quality deteriorates, replace the holder and ribbon as one unit.
In a dot matrix printer, the part whose column of pins strikes the ribbon against the paper; replace it by following the manufacturer's instructions, and take care, since it can get very hot.
Loading an impact printer: set the lever to friction feed for plain paper or to tractor feed for tractor-fed paper, making sure the paper's holes engage the sprockets so it feeds cleanly.
On a laser printer, dirty feed rollers or a dirty or damaged drum; on an inkjet, a dirty print head or blocked nozzle, so run a cleaning cycle; on a dot matrix, a stuck pin.
Many pages with a few characters, or blank pages, from a rendering fault; clear the queue and power cycle the printer, then update the driver and use a supported language like PCL or PostScript.

Paper stuck in the paper path, often from unsuitable, creased, or badly loaded media or faulty rollers; remove it gently without force, leave no torn pieces, and use the release levers in a laser printer's fuser.
On a laser printer, the toner cartridge likely needs replacing, unless a low-density (draft) option was selected; on a dot matrix, the platen gap between paper and print head may be too wide.
No sheet feeds in at all: check the paper's size, weight, loading, and media guides, and that it is not creased, damp, or dirty; if the media is fine, change the pickup rollers.
Feed rollers pull in two or more sheets at once; fan the stack to separate the sheets, and if the media is fine, change the pickup rollers, which come in a laser's maintenance kit.
A backed-up print queue, because the printer is offline, out of paper, or low on ink or toner, or one job hit an error; restart the stuck job, or delete it and try printing again.
Loose toner may be contaminating the paper in a laser printer; clean the printer's interior with an approved toner vacuum.

The image prints a second time on the page because the laser printer's photosensitive drum is not being cleaned properly; if printing different images does not clear it, replace the drum/toner cartridge.
On a laser printer, the toner cartridge, fuser, or gears/rollers: reseat parts, check for jams and debris, then replace the cartridge or maintenance kit; on an inkjet, a carriage mechanism fault.
Problems with the finisher unit that staples pages or punches holes on laser printers and multifunction devices; make sure the printer settings select the finisher as an installed output option.
Too many sheets can bend a staple and leave it stuck in the punch mechanism; remove the staple cartridge and release the catch to take out the stuck staples.
When a finisher punches holes, exceeding its maximum sheet count can cause jams; send print jobs in batches within that count, which may vary with paper weight.

A job printed portrait when it needs landscape, or the reverse, which can also put staples or binding in the wrong place; set the correct orientation and paper size, then test the settings on a short document.

Make sure the driver recognizes every installed tray and is updated, the tray is seated properly, and the right tray is selected in printer and driver settings; then power cycle the printer and computer.
The printer cannot be found or shows offline: check it is on and online, then print a test page from its control panel; if that works, check the cable, Wi-Fi network, and drivers.
New jobs cannot process; restart the Print Spooler service, clear the spooler cache by deleting the files in the spool folder while it is stopped, or delete a corrupt job.
